title: Complexity Analysis
summary: How to measure and reason about the cost of algorithms: growth rates, Big-O/Omega/Theta, analysing code, space, amortised analysis, recurrences and the Master Theorem, and what complexity means on real hardware.

lessons.title: Algorithms and counting work
lessons.summary: Count a scan with an explicit model of a basic operation.
lessons.body:
An **algorithm** is a finite, precise sequence of steps that takes some input and produces an output. "Sort this list", "find the shortest route", "check whether this password matches" all have algorithms behind them.

For this introductory discussion, a deterministic algorithm that correctly solves a total problem should be:

- **Well defined**: every step is unambiguous. "Pick a good pivot" is not a step; "pick the middle element" is.
- **Finite**: it terminates on every valid input.
- **Correct**: it produces the right output for every valid input, not just the ones you tried.

There are usually many correct algorithms for the same problem. This module is about how to compare them, and the main currency is **how the amount of work grows as the input grows**.

## Why not just time it?

The obvious way to compare two programs is to run them and use a stopwatch. That is useful (the later lessons on complexity in practice explain how to do it well), but on its own it tells you little:

- The result depends on the machine, the language, the compiler and what else was running.
- It tells you about the input you tried, not the input you will get next year.
- It does not tell you *why* one is faster, so it does not tell you how to make it faster.

Instead, we **count the basic operations** an algorithm performs as a function of the input size, usually called **n**. A basic operation is anything that takes a fixed amount of time regardless of n: an arithmetic step, a comparison, reading or writing one array element, the overhead of a function call (its body must be counted separately). Arithmetic and comparisons are constant-cost only for bounded-size values in this model.

This simplified machine, where each basic step costs one unit and memory access is uniform, is called the **RAM model**. It is not perfectly true of real hardware (the later lessons on complexity in practice show where it breaks), but it is close enough to predict which algorithm will win as n gets large.

## Counting operations

Here is a function that adds up a list:

```python
# total([2, 3, 5]) returns 10.
def total(xs):
    s = 0              # 1 op
    for x in xs:       # runs n times
        s += x         # 1 op per pass
    return s           # 1 op
```

Counting one operation per commented line gives a simple formula for the work:

```formula
T(n) = n + 2
T(1000) = 1000 + 2 = 1002
T_loop(n) = 2n + 2
where
T(n): the number of basic operations total() performs on a list of n items (a count of steps, not seconds)
n: the input size, here the number of items in the list xs; a whole number with no unit
T_loop(n): the operation count when each loop pass also charges one overhead step
In words: one operation for each item in the list, plus two more for setting s to 0 and returning it.
```

You could also count one extra loop-overhead step per pass, as the second cost in the card does. Either way, doubling the list doubles the work. That is what we care about.

## Key takeaways
- A correct algorithm for a total problem uses unambiguous steps and terminates on every valid input.
- Count operations against an explicitly stated input size.
- The running-total example does one addition per item; timings also depend on the environment.

## Further reading
- [Algorithm — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm)
- [Algorithms by Jeff Erickson (free textbook)](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/)
- [Erickson: Introduction](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/00-intro.pdf)

questions.prompt: Which properties are required of a deterministic algorithm that correctly solves a total problem for every valid input? Select all that apply.

options.text: Every step is precisely defined, with no ambiguity
options.explanation: Correct. 'Pick a good pivot' is not an algorithm step; 'pick the middle element' is. Unambiguous steps are part of the definition.

options.text: It finishes after a finite number of steps on every valid input
options.explanation: Correct. A procedure that can run forever on some valid input is not an algorithm for that problem.

options.text: It runs in polynomial time
options.explanation: Not required. An exponential-time brute-force search is still an algorithm, just a slow one. Efficiency is how we *compare* algorithms, not what makes something one.

options.text: It produces the correct output for every valid input
options.explanation: Correct. Working on the test cases you tried is not enough; correctness means all valid inputs.

options.text: It has been implemented in a programming language
options.explanation: Not required. Algorithms are abstract procedures; Euclid's algorithm for the greatest common divisor existed over two thousand years before computers.

questions.workedExample:
Check each option against the definition from the lesson: well defined, finite, correct.

1. Unambiguous steps: part of "well defined". Yes.
2. Terminates on every valid input: "finite". Yes.
3. Polynomial time: a statement about *efficiency*. Slow algorithms are still algorithms. No.
4. Correct on every valid input: "correct". Yes.
5. Implemented in code: an algorithm is the idea, not the program. No.

So the answer is the three properties: well defined, finite and correct.

lessons.title: Comparing every pair
lessons.summary: Count the comparisons in a duplicate check that visits each distinct pair once.
lessons.body:
The pairwise duplicate check shows why a small change in input length can create a large change in work. Here n is the number of list items.

## Counting pairs

Now a function that checks whether a list contains a duplicate by comparing every pair:

```python
# has_dup([2, 3, 2]) returns True.
def has_dup(xs):
    n = len(xs)
    for i in range(n):
        # Later positions: each pair once.
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if xs[i] == xs[j]:
                return True
    return False
```

In the worst case (no duplicates), how many comparisons? Here n is the item count; `i` and `j` are positions in the code. The first outer pass compares with every later position, the second skips one more position, and the final pass has no later positions. The series below records those shrinking counts.

```formula
C(n) = (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 + 0
C(n) = n(n − 1) / 2
C(5) = 5 × 4 / 2 = 10
C(1000) = 1000 × 999 / 2 = 499500
C(1000000) = 1000000 × 999999 / 2
C(1000000) = 499999500000
where
C(n): the number of comparisons has_dup makes in the worst case (no duplicates), on a list of n items
n: the number of items in the list; a whole number with no unit
…: "and so on": the terms keep falling by 1 until they reach 0
In words: every pair of different positions is compared exactly once, and a list of n items has n × (n − 1) / 2 pairs.
```

Where does the second line come from? Write the series forwards and backwards underneath itself. Each column totals one less than the item count, and there is one column per item. That counts every pair twice, so halve the product. Equivalently, pair every item with every other item and remove that same double count.

So for 5 items that is 10 comparisons, for 1,000 items 499,500, and for a million items about 500 billion, as the card shows. Doubling the list roughly **quadruples** the work: twice as many items, each compared with twice as many others.

A different approach sorts first and compares neighbours, since duplicates become adjacent. Good sorting algorithms take O(n log n) time, where n is the item count and log is the base-2 logarithm introduced next. A hash set gives O(n) expected time under the usual hashing assumptions. Same problem, three different growth rates.

## Key takeaways
- Compare each pair of distinct positions once.
- An early return helps some inputs; the no-duplicate input performs the full scan.
- Doubling the list approximately quadruples the pair count.

## Further reading
- [Analysis of algorithms — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analysis_of_algorithms)
- [Time complexity — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_complexity)

questions.prompt:
How many times does `print` run?

```python
# Later positions avoid repeated pairs.
for i in range(4):
    for j in range(i + 1, 4):
        print(i, j)
```

options.explanation: That would be two independent loops of 4 (4 x 4). Here the inner loop starts at `i + 1`, so it gets shorter each time; it is not a full square.
10 is 4 + 3 + 2 + 1, which counts the inner loop as if it started at `i` rather than `i + 1`, i.e. it includes the pairs where i equals j.

Correct. The inner loop runs three, two, one and zero times: one print per unordered pair of the four indices.

```formula
C = 4 × 3 / 2 = 6
where
C: the number of printed pairs
In words: The inner loop runs three, two, one and zero times: one print per unordered pair of the four indices.
```

Eight guesses half of the full sixteen-cell square. Unordered distinct pairs exclude self-pairs and repeated orderings, so the actual count is six.

```formula
C = 4 × 3 / 2 = 6
4 × 4 = 16
where
C: the distinct unordered-pair count
In words: Eight guesses half of the full sixteen-cell square. Unordered distinct pairs exclude self-pairs and repeated orderings, so the actual count is six.
```

questions.workedExample:
Count the inner loop for each value of `i`:

| i | j values | prints |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1, 2, 3 | 3 |
| 1 | 2, 3 | 2 |
| 2 | 3 | 1 |
| 3 | none | 0 |

The total is **6**.

In general, with n in place of 4, this pattern prints once per pair of different indices:

```formula
P(n) = n(n − 1) / 2
P(4) = 4 × 3 / 2 = 6
where
P(n): the number of print calls
n: the loop bound, here 4: how many indices there are
In words: n indices make n × (n − 1) / 2 different pairs, and each pair is printed once.
```

It is the same structure as the pairwise duplicate check in the lesson, so doubling the item count roughly quadruples the comparisons.

questions.prompt: Which of these functions do work that grows **quadratically** in n, the loop bound (the input size)? Select all that apply.

options.explanation:
Correct. Each outer pass runs the entire inner range.

```formula
W(n) = n^2
where
W: the number of calls to work
n: the whole-number loop bound
In words: Each outer pass runs the entire inner range.
```

options.text:
```python
# Two separate passes over the range.
for i in range(n):
    work()
for j in range(n):
    work()
```
options.explanation:
Not quadratic. Sequential passes add rather than multiply.

```formula
W(n) = n + n = 2n
where
W: the number of calls to work
n: the whole-number loop bound
In words: Not quadratic. Sequential passes add rather than multiply.
```

Correct. Shrinking dependent counts add to roughly half the square.

```formula
W(n) = 0 + 1 + … + (n − 1)
W(n) = n(n − 1)/2
where
W: the number of calls to work
n: the whole-number loop bound
…: "and so on" up to the last term
In words: Shrinking dependent counts add to roughly half the square.
```

Not quadratic. The inner bound is fixed at one hundred.

```formula
W(n) = 100n
where
W: the number of calls to work
n: the whole-number loop bound
In words: Not quadratic. The inner bound is fixed at one hundred.
```

Correct. Integer halving changes the coefficient and rounding, not the quadratic growth.

```formula
W(n) = n⌊n/2⌋ ≈ n^2/2
where
W: the number of calls to work
n: the whole-number loop bound
≈: approximately equal to; the half-bound loses at most one inner-loop iteration when n is odd
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down
In words: Integer halving changes the coefficient and rounding, not the quadratic growth.
```

questions.workedExample:
Here n is the loop bound in each snippet (the input size). Count calls to `work()` in each:

```formula
A = n × n = n^2
B = n + n = 2n
C = 0 + 1 + … + (n − 1)
C = n(n − 1) / 2
D = 100n = 100n
E = n⌊n / 2⌋ ≈ n^2 / 2
where
A, B, C, D, E: the number of work() calls made by options A to E
n: the input size, the bound of the outer loop
⌊x⌋: floor: round x down to the nearest whole number, matching Python integer division
≈: approximately equal to; the half-bound loses at most one inner-loop iteration when n is odd
…: "and so on" up to the last term
In words: A, C and E multiply n by something that grows with n, so they are quadratic; B and D multiply or add n by a constant, so they are linear.
```

| Code | Growth |
|---|---|
| A: n inside n | quadratic |
| B: two loops in a row | linear |
| C: inner to i | quadratic |
| D: inner fixed 100 | linear |
| E: half-size inner bound | quadratic |

The test: does the inner loop's length depend on n? If yes and it is nested, the counts multiply into quadratic growth. If the inner length is a constant, or the loops are sequential, it stays linear.

questions.prompt: A CSV validator checks for duplicate rows by comparing every pair. A customer uploads **2,000,000** rows. Assuming about 10^8 comparisons per second, roughly how long does the worst case (no duplicates) take?

options.text: About 0.02 seconds
options.explanation:
This is the hypothetical time for a linear scan, whereas the pairwise algorithm has quadratic work.

```formula
t = 2000000 / (10^8/s) = 0.02 s
where
s: seconds
t: the linear-scan time
In words: This is the hypothetical time for a linear scan, whereas the pairwise algorithm has quadratic work.
```

options.text: About 40 seconds
options.explanation:
This undercounts the squared row count by a thousandfold before dividing by the rate.

```formula
4000000000 / (10^8/s) = 40 s
2000000^2 = 4000000000000
where
s: seconds
In words: This undercounts the squared row count by a thousandfold before dividing by the rate.
```

options.text: About 5.6 hours
options.explanation:
Correct. Each unordered pair is compared once. Dividing the pair count by the assumed comparison rate gives the estimate.

```formula
C ≈ 2000000^2 / 2 = 2 × 10^12
t = C / (10^8/s) ≈ 20000 s
where
C: the pair-comparison count
s: seconds
t: the estimated time
≈: approximately equal to (n − 1 is treated as n)
In words: Each unordered pair is compared once. Dividing the pair count by the assumed comparison rate gives the estimate.
```

options.text: About 11 hours
options.explanation: This counts the whole square, forgetting that distinct unordered pairs halve the leading term. The full square is four trillion comparisons before halving.

questions.workedExample:
Count the comparisons, then divide by the speed:

```formula
C = n(n − 1) / 2
C ≈ (2 × 10^6)^2 / 2 = 2 × 10^12
t = C / r
t ≈ 2 × 10^12 / (10^8/s)
t ≈ 2 × 10^4 s
t ≈ 20000 s / (3600 s/h) ≈ 5.6 h
where
C: the number of comparisons in the worst case (no duplicates)
n: the number of rows, here 2,000,000 = 2 × 10^6
t: the running time, in seconds (s) and then hours (h)
r: the assumed speed, 10^8 comparisons per second
s: seconds
h: hours; 1 h = 3,600 s
≈: approximately equal to (n − 1 is treated as n)
In words: two million rows make about two trillion pairs, which takes about twenty thousand seconds, or 5.6 hours.
```

Sorting takes O(n log n), where n is row count, versus quadratic pair checking. Its illustrative count is roughly 42 million steps; it would stay under half a second only if those steps sustain the assumed throughput. A hash set has O(n) expected work under the usual model. Benchmark actual costs: the improvement is a different growth rate, not a faster server.

lessons.title: Comparing growth rates
lessons.summary: Compare logarithmic, linear, quadratic and exponential operation counts.
lessons.body:
## Growth rates

The function that describes how the operation count grows is the algorithm's **growth rate**. Before comparing them, two pieces of notation need decoding: the logarithm and the power.

A **logarithm** answers "how many times do I multiply 2 by itself to reach n?", or equivalently "how many times can I halve n before I get down to 1?". It is the reverse of raising 2 to a power:

```formula
2^10 = 1024
log_2(1024) = 10
log_2(2^k) = k
where
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n: the power you raise 2 to in order to get n; it grows very slowly (log_2 of a million is about 20)
k: any number used as a power
n: here, any positive number
In words: the base-2 logarithm undoes "2 to the power": since ten 2s multiplied together make 1,024, the base-2 log of 1,024 is 10.
```

Logarithms appear whenever an algorithm repeatedly halves its problem, as binary search does. In this module logarithms use base two unless another base is stated; later lessons show why the base rarely matters.

Here are the common growth rates side by side:

```formula
f(n) = n log_2(n)
f(1000) ≈ 1000 × 10 = 10^4
f(n) = n^2 = n × n
f(n) = 2^n
f(n) = log_2(n)
f(n) = n
where
f(n): the number of operations an algorithm with this growth rate does on an input of n items
n: the input size, a whole number of items
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n: the power you raise 2 to in order to get n (log_2(1000) ≈ 9.97)
2^n: n copies of 2 multiplied together
10^4: ten to the power 4, which is 10,000
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: each row of the table below is one choice of f; the table shows how many operations each one needs at three input sizes.
```

Values are rounded and logarithms are base two:

| Growth | 10 items | 1,000 items | Million items |
|---|---|---|---|
| Logarithmic | 3 | 10 | 20 |
| Linear | 10 | 1,000 | 1,000,000 |
| Linear times log | 33 | 10,000 | 20,000,000 |
| Quadratic | 100 | 1,000,000 | 1,000,000,000,000 |
| Exponential | 1,024 | about 10^301 | absurd |

Two things jump out.

First, **for small inputs, nothing matters much.** On 10 items, even exponential subset search needs only 1,024 steps. This is why a naive algorithm often works fine in testing.

Second, **for large n, the growth rate is everything.** Suppose a machine does about 10^8 simple operations per second (an illustrative assumed rate, not a general hardware benchmark). Turning an operation count into a time is a division:

```formula
t = W / r
t = 10^12 / (10^8/s) = 10^4 s
t = 10^4 s / (3600 s/h) ≈ 2.8 h
where
t: the running time, in seconds (s)
W: the number of operations the algorithm does; here n^2 = 10^12 for n = 10^6 items
r: the machine's speed, assumed to be 10^8 (100 million) simple operations per second
n: the input size, here a million items
s: seconds
h: hours; 1 h = 3,600 s
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: a trillion operations at a hundred million per second takes ten thousand seconds, nearly three hours.
```

The same division for the other growth rates gives these illustrative times for a million items:

| Growth | Operations | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Linear | 1,000,000 | 0.01 s |
| Linear times log | 20,000,000 | 0.2 s |
| Quadratic | 1,000,000,000,000 | about 2.8 hours |

The quadratic algorithm is not "a bit slower". It is the difference between instant and unusable.

> [!example] The production surprise
> A team writes the pairwise `has_dup` check for a feature that validates uploaded CSV files. In testing, files have 200 rows: 19,900 comparisons, unnoticeable. A customer uploads 2 million rows: about 2 x 10^12 comparisons. The request times out, retries, and takes the worker pool with it. Nothing was "wrong" with the code except its growth rate.

## Key takeaways
- Repeated halving produces logarithmic growth.
- Large inputs separate linear, linearithmic, quadratic and exponential work.
- The example timings use an illustrative operation rate; actual runtime requires measurement.

## Further reading
- [Analysis of algorithms — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analysis_of_algorithms)
- [Time complexity — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_complexity)

questions.prompt:
Two algorithms solve the same problem. For 1,000 input items, roughly how many operations does each model below require?

```formula
A(n) = n^2
B(n) = n log_2(n)
n = 1000
where
A: algorithm A’s approximate operation count
B: algorithm B’s approximate operation count
log_2: the base-2 logarithm of n: the power you raise 2 to in order to get n
n: the input item count
In words: Compare the square of item count with item count times its logarithm, first at a thousand items.
```

options.explanation:
Correct. Squaring gives a million operations, while the logarithm is about ten and the second count about ten thousand. B uses roughly a hundredth of A’s work.

```formula
1000^2 = 1000000
log_2(1000) ≈ 10
1000 log_2(1000) ≈ 10000
where
log_2: the base-2 logarithm of n: the power you raise 2 to in order to get n
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: Squaring gives a million operations, while the logarithm is about ten and the second count about ten thousand. B uses roughly a hundredth of A’s work.
```
This doubles the input instead of squaring it. Squaring one thousand gives one million, not two thousand.

This uses base ten. The problem’s base-two logarithm is about ten; changing the base changes a constant factor and therefore the numerical count.

```formula
log_10(1000) = 3
log_2(1000) ≈ 10
where
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
log_2: the base-2 logarithm of n: the power you raise 2 to in order to get n
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: This uses base ten. The problem’s base-two logarithm is about ten; changing the base changes a constant factor and therefore the numerical count.
```
This swaps the answers. The quadratic count grows faster than the linear-times-log count.

questions.workedExample:
Substitute an input count of 1,000 into each formula:

```formula
A = n^2 = 1000 × 1000 = 10^6
2^10 = 1024, so log_2(1000) ≈ 10
B = n log_2(n) ≈ 1000 × 10 = 10^4
A / B ≈ 100
n = 1000000
A = 10^12, B ≈ 2 × 10^7
A/B ≈ 50000
where
A: operations algorithm A does
B: operations algorithm B does
n: the input item count, with separate 1,000-item and million-item substitutions items
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n: the power you raise 2 to in order to get n
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: A does about a million operations, B about ten thousand, so B does about a hundred times less work at this size.
```

At a million items, the ratio is about 50,000: a trillion operations versus twenty million. The quadratic and linear-times-log counts keep separating. A handy binary anchor is that powers with exponents ten, twenty and thirty are close to a thousand, a million and a billion.

A handy anchor: powers of two at ten, twenty and thirty are about a thousand, a million and a billion respectively.

questions.prompt: A function that compares every pair of items takes **2 seconds** on 10,000 items. Roughly how long will it take on **40,000** items?

options.text: 8 seconds
options.explanation: This assumes the time grows linearly with the number of items (4 times the input, 4 times the time). Comparing every pair is quadratic, so the time grows with the square of the ratio.

options.text: 16 seconds
options.explanation: 16 is the scaling factor, not the answer. You still have to multiply it by the original 2 seconds.

options.text: About 2.2 seconds
options.explanation: This treats quadratic pair counting as logarithmic growth. Pair counts grow roughly with the square of item count.

options.text: 32 seconds
options.explanation:
Correct. Quadratic work scales by the square of the input ratio, assuming the per-comparison cost stays fixed.

```formula
R = 40000 / 10000 = 4
t_new ≈ 2 s R^2 = 32 s
where
R: the input-length ratio
s: seconds
t_new: the new running time
≈: approximately equal
In words: Quadratic work scales by the square of the input ratio, assuming the per-comparison cost stays fixed.
```

questions.workedExample:
A pairwise comparison visits every unordered distinct pair, so its count grows quadratically. Scale time by the square of the input-length ratio:

```formula
t_new = t_old × (n_new / n_old)^2
t_new = 2 s × (40000 / 10000)^2
t_new = 2 s × 4^2 = 2 s × 16 = 32 s
where
t_old: the measured time on the old input, 2 seconds (s)
t_new: the predicted time on the new input, in seconds (s)
n_old: the old number of items, 10,000
n_new: the new number of items, 40,000
n: the number of items being compared
s: seconds
In words: four times the items means sixteen times the pairs, so sixteen times the time.
```

The same ratio method applies to other growth shapes: a fourfold input makes linear work fourfold and cubic work sixty-fourfold; linear-times-log work grows a little more than fourfold. This assumes comparison costs stay fixed, which is roughly true until data no longer fits in cache.

lessons.title: What faster hardware buys
lessons.summary: Translate a hardware speedup into the input size each growth rate can handle.
lessons.body:
Keep the time budget fixed and ask how much larger the input can become. The growth rate decides how much value a faster machine provides.

## Faster hardware does not save you

It is tempting to think faster hardware fixes a slow algorithm. Here N is the old input limit and N_new the new one, with the same time budget. The table compares growth shapes for a **10-times-faster** machine.

| Growth | Original limit | New limit |
|---|---|---|
| Linear | original | ten times original |
| Quadratic | original | about 3.16 times original |
| Cubic | original | about 2.15 times original |
| Exponential | original | about 3.3 extra items |

Where do these numbers come from? Set the work the new machine can do in the same time equal to 10 times the old work, and solve for the new input size:

```formula
N_new^2 = 10N^2
N_new = √(10) × N ≈ 3.16N
2^{N_new} = 10 × 2^N
N_new = N + log_2(10) ≈ N + 3.3
N_new = 10N
N_new^3 = 10N^3
N_new = 10^{1/3}N ≈ 2.15N
where
N: the largest input the old machine can handle in the time budget
N_new: the largest input the 10-times-faster machine can handle in the same time
√(10): the square root of 10, the number that multiplied by itself gives 10, about 3.16
log_2(10): the base-2 logarithm of 10, the power you raise 2 to in order to get 10, about 3.32
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: for quadratic work, 10 times the speed buys only √10 ≈ 3.16 times the input; for exponential work, it buys only about 3 more items.
```

For a cubic algorithm the same steps give the cube root of 10, about 2.15. Better algorithms routinely give improvements of thousands or millions of times; hardware gives you a constant factor.

## Key takeaways
- A hardware speedup changes a constant factor in runtime.
- For quadratic work, the input gain follows the square root of the speed gain.
- Exponential search gains only a few extra items from a large constant speedup.

## Further reading
- [Analysis of algorithms — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analysis_of_algorithms)
- [Algorithms by Jeff Erickson (free textbook)](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/)

questions.prompt: A quadratic algorithm can process at most 50,000 items within its one-hour time budget. You move it to hardware that is **100 times faster**. What is the largest input it can now handle in an hour?

options.explanation: That would be true for a linear algorithm, where 100 times the speed gives 100 times the input. A quadratic algorithm only gains the square root of the speed-up.
This adds to input size, which is the characteristic speedup pattern for exponential work, rather than quadratic work.

Correct. A hundredfold work budget buys a tenfold input increase for a quadratic algorithm.

```formula
R = √(100) = 10
N_new = 50000R = 500000
where
N_new: the new maximum item count
R: the input multiplier
√: the nonnegative square root
In words: A hundredfold work budget buys a tenfold input increase for a quadratic algorithm.
```
This doubles the input. Doubling the input quadruples quadratic work, which only uses 4 times of the 100 times speed-up available.

questions.workedExample:
Write the hour's work for both machines and solve for the new input size:

```formula
W = c × 50000^2
cn^2 = 100W = 100c × 50000^2
n^2 = 100 × 50000^2
n = √(100) × 50000 = 500000
where
W: the number of operations the old machine does in an hour
c: the fixed number of operations per unit of n^2 (the algorithm's constant factor); it cancels out
n: the largest number of items the new, 100-times-faster machine can handle in an hour
√(100): the square root of 100, which is 10
In words: a quadratic algorithm turns 100 times more speed into only √100 = 10 times more input.
```

Hardware buys a 100 times constant factor; for quadratic work that turns into only 10 times more input.

A brute-force search tries every subset of its input. It handles 40 items in about a minute on your laptop. A cluster is **1,024 times faster**. Roughly how many items can it handle in the same minute?

```formula

n: the input item count
```

options.text: 50 items

options.text: 40,960 items

options.text: 1,280 items

Set the cluster's work in one minute equal to the number of subsets and solve for n:

```formula

2^n = 2^40 × 2^10 = 2^50
n = 50
1024 = 2^10
```

lessons.title: Input size and dominant terms
lessons.summary: Choose the right input measure and simplify a cost without forgetting its limits.
lessons.body:
## What "input size" means

n should measure whatever drives the work. Usually it is obvious, but not always:

- For a list or string, n is its length.
- For a graph, cost may depend on both vertices V and edges E; state both, as in O(V + E).
- For big-number arithmetic, count **digits** or bits rather than the value. Testing every divisor up to a number’s value is linear in that value but exponential in its bit length.
- For matrices, distinguish side length from entry count. A 1,000-by-1,000 matrix has a million entries.

The number-size point is easy to get wrong, so here it is as a formula:

```formula
b = ⌊log_2(N)⌋ + 1
N ≈ 2^b
2^64 ≈ 1.8 × 10^19
M = n^2
where
N: the value of the number being tested, for example 1,000,003
b: the input size: how many bits (binary digits) it takes to write N down
log_2(N): the base-2 logarithm of N, the power you raise 2 to in order to get N
⌊x⌋: floor: round x down to the nearest whole number
≈: approximately equal to; a 64-bit number can be as large as 2^64 − 1, about 1.8 × 10^19
M: the entry count of a square matrix
n: the matrix side length, in entries
In words: adding one bit doubles the largest value you can write, so a loop that runs once per unit of value runs about 2^b times: exponential in the number of bits.
```

When you describe an algorithm's cost, always say what n is.

## Why we ignore the small stuff

Precise pair counting quickly becomes tedious and depends on what counts as one operation. The card expands that count to show which term eventually dominates.

```formula
C(n) = n(n − 1) / 2
C(n) = 0.5n^2 − 0.5n
C(1000) = 500000 − 500
C(2n) ≈ 0.5 × 4n^2 ≈ 4C(n)
A(n) = 100n
B(n) = n^2
A(50) = 5000 > B(50) = 2500
where
C(n): the number of comparisons the pairwise duplicate check makes on n items
n: the number of items in the list
≈: approximately equal to (the small 0.5 × n term is ignored)
A(n): the linear alternative’s operation count
B(n): the quadratic alternative’s operation count
>: greater than
In words: the n-squared term is a thousand times bigger than the other term at n = 1,000, and doubling n multiplies it by four whatever the constant in front.
```

1. **Keep only the fastest-growing term.** The quadratic part dominates the linear correction: at 1,000 items their contributions are 500,000 and 500.
2. **Drop constant factors.** Half the square and three times the square have the same doubling behaviour. Their constants depend on the machine and counting model; their growth shape does not.

The result is a coarse but robust label: "this algorithm is quadratic". The following asymptotic-notation lessons make this precise with Big-O, Big-Omega and Big-Theta.

> [!warning] Constants are not irrelevant in practice
> Dropping constants compares growth; it does not mean constants never matter. The card’s linear alternative loses to the quadratic one below 100 items, including its 50-item example. The later practice lessons explain when constants and hardware decide the winner.

## Key takeaways
- For integers, input size usually counts bits or digits rather than the represented value.
- State separate dimensions when several quantities drive the work.
- Dominant terms predict growth; constants can still decide the winner for small inputs.

## Further reading
- [Analysis of algorithms — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analysis_of_algorithms)
- [Time complexity — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_complexity)

options.text: Linear in the input size, so fast for any 64-bit number
options.explanation:
The loop is linear in numeric value, while input size is bit count. A prime near the stated scale needs roughly nine quintillion iterations, which is centuries under the illustrative throughput model.

```formula
N ≈ 2^63 ≈ 9.2 × 10^18
where
N: the prime’s numeric value
≈: approximately equal to
In words: The loop is linear in numeric value, while input size is bit count. A prime near the stated scale needs roughly nine quintillion iterations, which is centuries under the illustrative throughput model.
```

options.text: Logarithmic, because it returns as soon as it finds a divisor
options.explanation: Early exit helps for composite numbers with small factors, but when N is prime the loop runs all N - 2 times. Cost is judged on the worst case here.

options.text: Constant time, because a 64-bit number has a fixed size
options.explanation: A literally fixed finite input domain admits a constant upper bound, but that hides the huge practical cost. The question asks how work grows when bit width varies.

options.text: Linear in numeric value, exponential in bit count
options.explanation:
Correct. Adding bits doubles the largest representable value. Work proportional to that value is exponential in bit count.

```formula
N ≈ 2^b
where
N: the numeric value
b: the input bit count
≈: approximately equal to
In words: Adding bits doubles the largest representable value. Work proportional to that value is exponential in bit count.
```

questions.workedExample:
1. What is the input size? For a number, it is the number of digits or bits needed to write it, not its value.
2. The loop runs up to N − 2 times when N is prime. Convert that into bits and then into time:

```formula
b = ⌊log_2(N)⌋ + 1
N ≈ 2^b
N ≈ 2^63 ≈ 9.2 × 10^18
t ≈ 9.2 × 10^18 / (10^8/s)
≈ 9.2 × 10^10 s
√(N) ≈ 2^{b/2}
b = 63: 2^{b/2} ≈ 3 × 10^9
t ≈ 3 × 10^9 / (10^8/s) = 30 s
where
N: the number being tested for primality
b: the input size: how many bits it takes to write N
log_2(N): the base-2 logarithm of N, the power you raise 2 to in order to get N
⌊x⌋: floor: round x down to a whole number
2^b: b copies of 2 multiplied together
t: the worst-case running time, in seconds (s), at an assumed 10^8 loop iterations per second
s: seconds
≈: approximately equal to
√: the nonnegative square root
In words: each extra bit doubles N and so doubles the loop count; a 64-bit prime near 2^63 needs about 9 × 10^10 seconds, nearly 3,000 years.
```

Testing divisors only up to the square root cuts the exponent in half, as the card shows. At 63 bits it still needs roughly three billion iterations: about thirty seconds only under the hypothetical hundred-million-divisions-per-second model. It remains exponential in bit count. Algorithms polynomial in numeric value but exponential in bit length are **pseudo-polynomial**.

Algorithm A and B have the exact operation counts below. Below roughly what input size is **B** faster? Consider whole-number inputs of at least two items.

```formula
A(n) = 100n log_2(n)
B(n) = n^2
n ≥ 2
where
A: algorithm A’s exact operation count
B: algorithm B’s exact operation count
log_2: the base-2 logarithm of n, the power you raise 2 to in order to get n (log_2(1000) ≈ 9.97)
n: the input size (number of items), a whole number of at least 2
<, >, ≤, ≥: less than, greater than, at most, at least
In words: One algorithm has a hundredfold coefficient on linear-times-log work; the other has quadratic work.
```

options.text: About 100 items
options.explanation:
B is still well ahead at one hundred items; the crossover is further out.

```formula
A(100) ≈ 100 × 100 × 6.64 = 66400
B(100) = 100^2 = 10000
where
A: A’s exact operation count
B: B’s exact operation count
≈: approximately equal to
In words: B is still well ahead at one hundred items; the crossover is further out.
```

options.text: About 1,000 items
options.explanation:
Correct. B wins while its squared count is below A’s scaled linear-times-log count. The card evaluates the boundary near a thousand items.

```formula
n^2 < 100n log_2(n)
n < 100 log_2(n)
100 log_2(1000) ≈ 997
where
log_2: the base-2 logarithm of n, the power you raise 2 to in order to get n (log_2(1000) ≈ 9.97)
n: the input size (number of items), a whole number of at least 2
≈: approximately equal to
<, >, ≤, ≥: less than, greater than, at most, at least
In words: B wins while its squared count is below A’s scaled linear-times-log count. The card evaluates the boundary near a thousand items.
```

options.text: About 10,000 items
options.explanation:
By ten thousand items, A is already about seven and a half times faster.

```formula
100 log_2(10000) ≈ 1329
10000 / 1329 ≈ 7.5
where
log_2: the base-2 logarithm of n, the power you raise 2 to in order to get n (log_2(1000) ≈ 9.97)
≈: approximately equal to
In words: By ten thousand items, A is already about seven and a half times faster.
```

options.text: B is never faster because quadratic growth is worse
options.explanation: Asymptotic comparison only says A wins *eventually*. With a constant of 100, B wins for every input size below the crossover. This is why constants matter in practice.

questions.workedExample:
B is faster while its operation count is smaller. Write that as an inequality and simplify:

```formula
n^2 < 100n log_2(n)
n < 100log_2(n)
n = 1000:  100log_2(n) ≈ 997 < n
where
n: the input size (number of items), a whole number of at least 2
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n, the power you raise 2 to in order to get n (log_2(1000) ≈ 9.97)
<: is less than
≈: approximately equal to
In words: dividing both sides by n shows B wins while n is smaller than 100 times its own base-2 log, which stops being true just below n = 1,000.
```

Try values:

| Items | Scaled log value | B faster? |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 664 | yes |
| 900 | 981 | yes |
| 1,000 | 997 | no, just |
| 10,000 | 1,329 | no |

The crossover is just under 1,000 items.

The lesson's point: a large constant can make the asymptotically worse algorithm the better choice for small inputs. Real sorting libraries exploit exactly this.

questions.prompt: An image library documents its blur filter as taking time proportional to N, the number of pixels. You switch from 1080p (1920 x 1080) images to 4K (3840 x 2160). How does the blur time change?

options.text: It quadruples
options.explanation:
Correct. Doubling both dimensions quadruples pixel count. Runtime is linear in pixels but quadratic in side length at a fixed aspect ratio.

```formula
N_old = 1920 × 1080
N_new = 3840 × 2160 = 4N_old
where
N_new: the new pixel count
N_old: the old pixel count
In words: Doubling both dimensions quadruples pixel count. Runtime is linear in pixels but quadratic in side length at a fixed aspect ratio.
```

options.text: It doubles, because the resolution doubled
options.explanation: Each *side* doubled, but the filter's cost is in pixels. Doubling both width and height multiplies the pixel count by 4.

options.text: Sixteen-fold: a square image makes the filter quadratic
options.explanation: This squares twice. The filter is linear in pixels, and pixels already grow with the square of the side. 2 times the side gives 4 times the pixels gives 4 times the time.

options.text: It stays the same, because the filter is linear
options.explanation: 'Linear' describes how time grows with N; it does not mean constant. N has quadrupled.

questions.workedExample:
1. What is the input size? The documentation counts pixels rather than side length.
2. Compute the pixel counts and their ratio:

```formula
N_old = 1920 × 1080 = 2073600
N_new = 3840 × 2160 = 8294400
N_new / N_old = 4
where
N_old: the number of pixels in a 1080p image
N_new: the number of pixels in a 4K image
N: the number of pixels, which the blur's time is proportional to
In words: doubling both the width and the height gives four times as many pixels, so a filter whose time is proportional to the pixel count takes four times as long.
```

The same algorithm is "linear" in pixels and "quadratic" in side length. Neither is wrong; you just have to say which input size you mean.

lessons.title: Proving an upper bound
lessons.summary: Use fixed constants to prove or disprove a Big-O claim.
lessons.body:
The last lesson said we keep the fastest-growing term and drop constants. **Asymptotic notation** is the precise language for doing that. It describes how a function behaves as n, the input size, grows towards infinity, which is why it is called *asymptotic*.

There are three main symbols. Think of them as comparisons between growth rates, where f and g are two functions of n:

| Notation | Read as | Pointwise analogy |
|---|---|---|
| Big-O | upper growth bound | no greater than |
| Big-Omega | lower growth bound | no smaller than |
| Big-Theta | tight growth bound | equality |

O is the capital letter O ("Big-O"), Ω is Greek capital omega and Θ is Greek capital theta. Here f is the exact operation-count function and g a simpler comparison function, often quadratic. These labels compare eventual growth, rather than literal pointwise inequalities.

## Big-O: an upper bound

**Definition.** Big-O says f is eventually no bigger than a fixed multiple of g:

```formula
f(n) = O(g(n))  means:
0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c g(n)  for all n ≥ n_0
where
f(n): the algorithm’s operation-count function
g(n): the simpler comparison function
n: the input size, a whole number
O(g(n)): functions eventually bounded by a fixed multiple of g(n)
c: a chosen fixed positive multiplier, independent of input size
n_0: the chosen input threshold where the bound starts
≤, ≥: less than or equal to, greater than or equal to
In words: beyond some starting point n_0, f never exceeds a fixed multiple of g.
```

The two constants are what let us ignore details. c absorbs constant factors (a faster machine, a different way of counting). n_0 lets us ignore small inputs, where odd things can happen.

### Proving a Big-O bound

To prove a Big-O claim, find fixed constants that make its definition true. The example below bounds a quadratic polynomial by replacing its smaller terms with quadratic terms, which only increases the right-hand side.

```formula
f(n) = 3n^2 + 5n + 2
f(n) ≤ 3n^2 + 5n^2 + 2n^2
f(n) ≤ 10n^2   for n ≥ 1
n ≤ n^2 and 1 ≤ n^2 for n ≥ 1
c = 10, n_0 = 1
f(100) / 100^2 = 30502 / 10000 ≈ 3.05
where
f(n): the exact operation count being bounded
n: the input size, a whole number of at least 1
≤, ≥: less than or equal to, greater than or equal to
c: the fixed upper-bound multiplier
n_0: the first input size for the bound
≈: approximately equal
In words: once n is at least 1, f(n) is never more than 10 times n^2, so c = 10 and n_0 = 1 prove that f(n) = O(n^2).
```

These constants work. Any larger multiplier or starting threshold also works; one pair suffices.

A quick table confirms it:

| Items | Exact count | Upper limit |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10 | 10 |
| 2 | 24 | 40 |
| 10 | 352 | 1,000 |
| 100 | 30,502 | 100,000 |

The ratio of the polynomial to the square settles towards 3. The card evaluates it at 100 items, giving about 3.05. A multiplier of 10 is loose, but loose is fine for Big-O.

### Disproving one

To disprove a Big-O claim, show that no fixed constants can work. A quadratic function is **not** O(n), where n is the input size. Suppose that bound were possible:

```formula
n^2 ≤ cn   for all n ≥ n_0
n ≤ c   for all n ≥ n_0
for every c > 0 and every n_0:
some n ≥ n_0: f(n) > cg(n)
where
n: the input size, a positive whole number
c: the fixed positive constant the definition of O(n) would need
n_0: the threshold input size the definition would need
≤, ≥: less than or equal to, greater than or equal to
O(n): Big-O of n: functions eventually at most a constant times n
f(n): the count whose proposed upper bound is being disproved
g(n): the eventually positive comparison function
>: greater than
In words: division by positive input forces that input below a fixed multiplier forever, a contradiction. Generally, every proposed multiplier and threshold must fail at some later input.
```

But n keeps growing and c is fixed, so this fails as soon as n is bigger than c. Contradiction.

A ratio tending to infinity disproves an upper bound for an eventually positive comparison function. It is sufficient, not necessary: ratios can oscillate. The card’s final condition gives the general negation.

## Key takeaways
- An upper bound eventually holds with one fixed multiplier.
- Proving a bound means choosing constants that work for every sufficiently large input.
- A valid upper bound may be looser than useful.

## Further reading
- [Big O notation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation)
- [Algorithms by Jeff Erickson (free textbook)](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/)

questions.prompt:
You want to prove a linear upper bound for the cost below. Which listed multiplier/starting-threshold pairs work? Select all that apply.

```formula
f(n) = 5n + 20
f(n) ≤ cn for all n ≥ n_0
where
c: the positive fixed upper-bound multiplier
n: the positive item count
f: the operation count
n_0: the first input size at which the bound must hold
<, >, ≤, ≥: less than, greater than, at most, at least
In words: A valid upper bound must use one fixed multiplier and hold at every input beyond the proposed threshold.
```

options.text: Multiplier 6; threshold 20
options.explanation:
Works. The required inequality begins at twenty items, exactly the supplied threshold.

```formula
5n + 20 ≤ 6n means n ≥ 20
where
n: the input size, a positive whole number
<, >, ≤, ≥: less than, greater than, at most, at least
In words: Works. The required inequality begins at twenty items, exactly the supplied threshold.
```

options.text: Multiplier 5; threshold 100
options.explanation:
Fails. Matching the leading coefficient leaves an impossible positive constant on the left.

```formula
5n + 20 ≤ 5n means 20 ≤ 0
where
n: the input size, a positive whole number
<, >, ≤, ≥: less than, greater than, at most, at least
In words: Fails. Matching the leading coefficient leaves an impossible positive constant on the left.
```

options.text: Multiplier 25; threshold 1
options.explanation:
Works. The larger multiplier absorbs the constant from the first positive input.

```formula
5n + 20 ≤ 25n means n ≥ 1
where
n: the input size, a positive whole number
<, >, ≤, ≥: less than, greater than, at most, at least
In words: Works. The larger multiplier absorbs the constant from the first positive input.
```

options.text: Multiplier 6; threshold 10
options.explanation:
Fails. The multiplier is sufficient, but the threshold is too early.

```formula
n = 10: 5n + 20 = 70 > 6n = 60
where
n: the input size, a positive whole number
<, >, ≤, ≥: less than, greater than, at most, at least
In words: Fails. The multiplier is sufficient, but the threshold is too early.
```

Fails. This multiplier is below the leading coefficient, so no later threshold rescues it.

```formula
where
n: the input size, a positive whole number
<, >, ≤, ≥: less than, greater than, at most, at least
In words: Fails. This multiplier is below the leading coefficient, so no later threshold rescues it.
```

questions.workedExample:
Rearrange the inequality to see which n it holds for:

```formula
5n + 20 ≤ cn
20 ≤ (c − 5) × n
n ≥ 20 / (c − 5)   (when c > 5)
where
n: the input size, a positive whole number
c: the constant in the Big-O definition, which you choose
≤, ≥: less than or equal to, greater than or equal to
In words: subtract 5n from both sides; if c is above 5 you can divide by c − 5 to find the smallest n that works.
```

- A multiplier no greater than the leading coefficient cannot absorb the positive constant. This rules out multipliers five and one.
- A larger multiplier works once the rearranged threshold in the card is reached.

Check the candidates:

| Multiplier | Required threshold | Given threshold | Works? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | 20 | 20 | yes |
| 6 | 20 | 10 | no |
| 25 | 1 | 1 | yes |

questions.prompt: In a code review, you write that a binary search over n items is `O(n)`. A colleague says that is wrong because binary search is `O(log n)`, where log denotes the base-two logarithm. Who is right?

options.text: Both statements are true, but O(log n) is the tighter and more useful one
options.explanation:
Correct. A logarithmic bound also has a linear upper bound. The latter is true but loose; report the tightest useful bound. Here n is item count.

```formula
log_2(n) ≤ n for n ≥ 1
where
log_2: the base-2 logarithm of n, about the number of halvings
n: the number of items being searched
<, >, ≤, ≥: less than, greater than, at most, at least
In words: A logarithmic bound also has a linear upper bound. The latter is true but loose; report the tightest useful bound. Here n is item count.
```

options.text: The colleague: an algorithm has exactly one Big-O
options.explanation: Big-O is an upper bound, and any function that grows at least as fast as the true cost is a valid upper bound. An algorithm belongs to many O classes.

options.text: You are: O(n) is safer because it covers the worst case
options.explanation: Binary search's worst case is still Θ(log n). O(n) is not 'safer', just less informative. Here n is the input item count.

options.text: Neither: binary search is Θ(1) in the best case, so its Big-O is O(1)
options.explanation: The best case (target found at the first midpoint) is Θ(1), but O bounds the cost from above over the inputs you are discussing. O(1) is not an upper bound on the worst case.

questions.workedExample:
1. Binary search halves the range each step, so its worst-case cost is Θ(log n): a logarithmic number of halvings.
2. Big-O is an upper bound, and its logarithm never exceeds the positive input size:

```formula
f(n) = O(g(n)) if f(n) ≤ c g(n)
log_2(n) ≤ n   for all n ≥ 1
where
f(n): the cost being bounded, here the search's step count
g(n): the bounding function
O(g(n)): Big-O: eventually at most a constant times g(n)
c: a fixed positive constant (c = 1 is enough here)
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n, about the number of halvings
n: the number of items being searched
≤, ≥: less than or equal to, greater than or equal to
In words: the logarithm of n is never bigger than n, so a cost bounded by log n is also bounded by n.
```

3. So the search is also O(n), and O(n^2), and O(2^n).
4. All true, increasingly useless.

Takeaway: when people say "O" in practice they mean the tight bound. Saying Θ(log n) removes the ambiguity.

lessons.title: Lower and tight bounds
lessons.summary: Distinguish lower bounds, tight bounds and input cases.
lessons.body:
Here n is the input size. A lower bound and a tight bound add information that an upper bound alone cannot provide.

## Big-Omega: a lower bound

**Definition.** Big-Omega is the mirror image: f is eventually at least a fixed positive multiple of g.

```formula
f(n) = Ω(g(n))  means:
f(n) ≥ c g(n) ≥ 0  for all n ≥ n_0
f(n) = 3n^2 + 5n + 2
f(n) ≥ 3n^2 for n ≥ 0
c = 3
where
f(n): the function being described, usually an operation count
g(n): the simple comparison function
n: the input size, a whole number
Ω(g(n)): Big-Omega of g (Ω is the Greek capital omega): the set of functions that are eventually at least a positive constant times g(n)
c: some fixed positive constant (c > 0) that does not depend on n
n_0: a threshold input size; the inequality must hold from there on
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: beyond some starting point, f never drops below a fixed fraction of g.
```

The quadratic polynomial from the upper-bound example also has a quadratic lower bound: its remaining terms are nonnegative. The example follows the definition below.

Omega is used to say "at least this much work is unavoidable". A famous example you will meet later: any sorting algorithm that only compares elements needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case, where n is the number of items being sorted.

## Big-Theta: a tight bound

**Definition.** Big-Theta says f is squeezed between two multiples of g, so it is both O(g) and Ω(g):

```formula
f(n) = Θ(g(n))  means:
c_1 × g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c_2 × g(n)
for all n ≥ n_0
3n^2 ≤ 3n^2 + 5n + 2 ≤ 10n^2
c_1 = 3, c_2 = 10, n_0 = 1
where
f(n): the function being described, usually an operation count
g(n): the simple comparison function
n: the input size, a whole number
Θ(g(n)): Big-Theta of g (Θ is the Greek capital theta): functions that grow at the same rate as g(n), up to constant factors
c_1: a fixed positive constant for the lower bound
c_2: a fixed positive constant for the upper bound
n_0: a threshold input size; both inequalities must hold from there on
≤, ≥: less than or equal to, greater than or equal to
In words: beyond some point, f stays between two fixed multiples of g, so it grows at exactly g's rate.
```

The same polynomial is squeezed between the two quadratic multiples below. This makes Theta the most informative statement: it pins growth down up to constants.

> [!note] Industry "Big-O" usually means Theta
> Strictly, O is only an upper bound. Binary search on n items is O(log n), but it is also O(n) and O(n^2), because those are bigger. All true, the last two useless. When engineers say "this is O(n)", they almost always mean "this is Θ(n)": the bound is tight. In interviews and code reviews, give the tightest bound you can.

## Not every function has a tidy Theta

Consider a function doing one step on odd input sizes and as many steps as the input size on even sizes. It is O(n) and Ω(1), where n is the input size, but neither Θ(n) nor Θ(1). A tight bound still exists: every function has its own growth rate as a tight bound, or use that same piecewise cost as the comparison. It simply does not match a familiar monotone growth class.

## Big-O is not "worst case"

A very common confusion. **O, Ω and Θ describe functions. Best, average and worst case describe which input you are talking about.** They are independent. For insertion sort on n items:

- Its worst-case time is Θ(n^2).
- Its best-case time (already-sorted input) is Θ(n).
- So its running time overall is O(n^2) and Ω(n).

You can put a Θ on the worst case, an O on the average case, and so on. The code-analysis lessons cover cases in detail.

## Key takeaways
- A tight bound combines an upper and lower bound for the same cost function.
- Best, average and worst cases describe inputs; asymptotic notation describes the resulting functions.
- An irregular function need not fit a familiar monotone growth class.

## Further reading
- [Big O notation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation)
- [Asymptotic analysis — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asymptotic_analysis)

lessons.title: Simplifying asymptotic expressions
lessons.summary: Drop dominated terms while preserving distinctions between exponential bases.
lessons.body:
Here n is the input size. These rules simplify a cost after the meaning of upper, lower and tight bounds is clear.

## Simplification rules

These all follow from the definitions. In each, n is the input size:

- **Constants vanish.** Fixed multipliers go into the bound’s constant.
- **Sums take the maximum.** Eventually the fastest-growing term dwarfs the others.
- **Log bases do not matter.** Any two logarithms differ by a fixed factor, so O(log n) ignores their bases.
- **Exponent bases do matter.** Cubic-base and quartic-base exponentials outgrow a base-two exponential.
- **Polynomials beat logs, exponentials beat polynomials.** The examples below hold eventually even when small inputs suggest the reverse.
- **Products multiply.** Θ(n) iterations each costing Θ(log n) give Θ(n log n) overall. Here n is the input size.

```formula
5n^2 = Θ(n^2)
n^3 + 100n^2 + 10^6 = Θ(n^3)
(log(n))^{100} = o(n^{0.01})
n^{100} = o(1.01^n)
where
n: the input size
log: the base-2 logarithm
Θ: a tight growth bound
o: little-o: grows strictly slower than the comparison
In words: Fixed coefficients and dominated terms do not change eventual growth. A fixed power of a logarithm loses to any positive power of the input, and a fixed polynomial loses to an exponential.
```

Why log bases don't matter: the change-of-base rule turns a log in one base into a log in another by dividing by a constant.

```formula
log_a(n) = log_b(n) / log_b(a)
log_2(n) = log_10(n) / log_10(2)
log_2(n) ≈ 3.32log_10(n)
where
log_a(n): the logarithm of n to base a: the power you raise a to in order to get n
log_b(n): the logarithm of n to base b
log_b(a): the logarithm of a to base b, a fixed number because a and b are fixed
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n
log_10(n): the base-10 logarithm of n (log_10(1000) = 3)
a, b: any two fixed bases greater than 1
n: the input size
≈: approximately equal to
In words: switching the base of a logarithm just multiplies it by a constant, and Big-O ignores constants, so O(log_2 n) and O(log_10 n) are the same class.
```

Why exponent bases do matter: dividing one exponential by another leaves an exponential, not a constant.

```formula
3^n / 2^n = (3 / 2)^n = 1.5^n
4^n = (2^2)^n = 2^{2n}
4^n / 2^n = 2^n
where
2^n: n copies of 2 multiplied together
n: the input size
In words: the ratio of two exponentials with different bases keeps growing, so no constant c can cover it and the faster one is not Big-O of the slower one.
```

> [!warning] The "=" is one-way
> A growth class is a set of functions. Saying a function has an upper bound means membership in that set, rather than ordinary equality. Reversing that statement treats a class as a value. Two functions in the same class need not equal one another.

```formula
f ∈ O(g)
n ∈ O(n^2)
f ∈ O(n^2), g ∈ O(n^2)
f(n) = n, g(n) = n^2
f ≠ g
where
f, g: operation-count functions; the last two lines give a counterexample with f linear and g quadratic
f(n), g(n): the values of those functions at input size n
n: the positive input size; in the second line n names the linear input-size function
O: an eventual upper growth class
∈: is a member of
≠: is not equal to
In words: Membership is not equality: a linear function has a quadratic upper bound, and two functions can share a bound without having equal values.
```

An expression that incorrectly treats the class as a number is:

```formula
O(n^2) = n
where
n: the input size
O(n^2): the class of functions with a quadratic upper bound
In words: This displayed equality is invalid; it reverses a membership statement and compares a class with a value.
```

## Key takeaways
- Constants and lower-order terms disappear when comparing eventual growth.
- Changing a logarithm base changes a constant factor.
- Changing an exponential base can change the growth class.

## Further reading
- [Big O notation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation)
- [Asymptotic analysis — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asymptotic_analysis)

lessons.title: Ordering growth with limits
lessons.summary: Use ratios and the growth ladder to compare unfamiliar cost functions.
lessons.body:
Here n is the input size; logarithms use base 2 unless a different base is stated. Use the simplification rules and ratio limits together.

## The limit test

A quick way to compare two functions is to look at what their ratio does as n grows without limit:

```formula
L = lim_{n→∞} f(n) / g(n)
L = 0: f(n) = O(g(n))
L = 0: f(n) = o(g(n))
L = 0: f(n) ∉ Ω(g(n))
0 < L < ∞: f(n) = Θ(g(n))
L = ∞: f(n) = Ω(g(n))
L = ∞: f(n) ∉ O(g(n))
where
L: the value the ratio settles towards
lim_{n→∞}: "the limit as n tends to infinity": the value f(n) / g(n) gets closer and closer to as n grows without bound
n: the input size
f(n), g(n): the two functions being compared, both positive for large n
∞: infinity: growing without any upper limit
→: "tends to", "heads towards"
O: an eventual upper growth bound
Ω: an eventual lower growth bound
Θ: matching upper and lower growth bounds
o: strictly slower growth
∉: is not a member of the indicated growth class
<: less than
In words: divide one function by the other and watch what the answer heads towards as n gets enormous.
```

| Ratio limit | Conclusion |
|---|---|
| Zero | upper bound, no lower bound |
| Finite positive constant | tight bound |
| Infinity | lower bound, no upper bound |

For example, compare the linear and quadratic functions in the following substitution:

```formula
f(n) / g(n) = n / n^2 = 1 / n
1 / n → 0   as n → ∞
f(n) = n, g(n) = n^2
where
f(n): here n, a linear function
g(n): here n^2, n × n
n: the input size
→: "tends to"
∞: infinity, growing without limit
In words: n divided by n squared shrinks towards zero, so n grows strictly slower than n squared.
```

The linear function therefore has a quadratic upper bound but no quadratic tight bound. A zero ratio limit is also called **little-o**: strictly slower growth. The limit test only works when a limit exists; for oscillating functions, return to the definitions.

## The ladder of common classes

From slowest to fastest, these classes use n for input size. Logarithms are base two, a square root means the nonnegative root, and factorial is the product of all positive integers up to the item count. Most example algorithms are studied later.

| Class | Name | Example |
|---|---|---|
| O(1) | constant | array index |
| O(log n) | logarithmic | binary search |
| O(√n) | square root | divisors up to the square root |
| O(n) | linear | scan a list |
| O(n log n) | linearithmic | merge sort |
| O(n^2) | quadratic | all pairs |
| O(n^3) | cubic | naive matrix multiply |
| O(2^n) | exponential | all subsets |
| O(n!) | factorial | all orderings |

A few points worth knowing:

- **O(1)** means bounded by a constant, not "one step". Reading 1,000 fixed fields is still O(1).
- **O(log n)** is what you get by repeatedly halving the problem. The base-2 log of a billion is about 30, because 2^30 ≈ 1.07 billion.
- **Factorial** grows faster than any exponential with a fixed base. Stirling’s approximation gives its size; taking its logarithm gives the comparison-sorting lower bound:

```formula
n! = n(n − 1) × … × 2 × 1
log(n!) = Θ(n log(n))
20! ≈ 2.4 × 10^18
25! ≈ 1.6 × 10^25
where
n!: n factorial: the number of different orders n items can be arranged in
n: a whole number, here the number of items
…: "and so on": every whole number in between
log: the logarithm (base 2 here; the base only changes a constant)
Θ: Big-Theta: grows at the same rate as, up to constant factors
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the number of orderings of n items is astronomically large, but its logarithm grows only like n log n.
```

- **Multiple variables** are fine and often necessary. A graph algorithm might be O(V + E), where V is the number of vertices and E the number of edges; joining two lists of lengths n and m might be O(n + m). Do not collapse them into one n unless you know how they relate.

## Key takeaways
- A ratio limit compares growth when that limit exists.
- Polynomial, exponential and factorial functions can be ordered by their eventual growth.
- The logarithm of a factorial grows like the item count times its logarithm.

## Further reading
- [Big O notation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation)
- [Stirling's approximation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling%27s_approximation)

lessons.title: Counting sequential and nested loops
lessons.summary: Add sequential work and count the true length of dependent inner loops.
lessons.body:
You now have the notation. This lesson is about using it: looking at a piece of code and working out its time complexity quickly and correctly. Most code reduces to a handful of patterns, plus a few traps that catch even experienced engineers.

Throughout, n is the input size (for example the length of the list), and m is the size of a second input when there is one. O(...) is Big-O, an upper bound on growth; Θ(...) is Big-Theta, a tight bound; and logarithms use base two, roughly how many times you can halve n before reaching 1.

## The basic rules

1. **Cost model.** Treat fixed-size arithmetic, comparison and indexing as O(1). Python arbitrary-precision integers, long strings, user-defined comparisons and output can cost more; the counts below abstract those costs unless stated otherwise.
2. **Sequential blocks add.** A linear block followed by a quadratic block has quadratic overall growth, because the quadratic term dominates.
3. **Nested independent loops multiply.** O(n) iterations, each doing O(m) work, give O(nm), where n and m are the separate input sizes.
4. **Branches take the worse side.** For the worst case, choose the more expensive branch.
5. **Function calls cost whatever the function costs.** A one-line call to `sorted()` is O(n log n), where n is the list length.

Those cover simple code. The interesting cases are loops whose bounds change.

## Dependent nested loops

When the inner loop depends on the outer variable, you have to **sum** rather than multiply.

```python
# work() means one constant-cost step.
for i in range(n):
    # The inner loop's length depends on i.
    for j in range(i):
        work()
```

The inner loop lengths rise from zero to one less than the outer bound. Add those lengths:

```formula
W(n) = 0 + 1 + 2 + … + (n − 1)
W(n) = Σ_{i=0}^{n−1} i
W(n) = n(n − 1) / 2 = Θ(n^2)
W(10) = 10 × 9 / 2 = 45
where
W(n): the number of times work() runs
n: the input size, the bound of the outer loop
i: the outer loop's counter; on pass i the inner loop runs i times
Σ_{i=0}^{n−1}: capital sigma, "sum of": add up the expression after it for every whole number i from 0 to n − 1
…: "and so on" up to the last term
Θ(n^2): Big-Theta of n squared: grows at exactly the rate of n × n, up to a constant factor
In words: the inner loop runs once more on each pass, the runs add up to about half of n squared, and halving does not change the growth class.
```

Halving the work does not change the class.

Three nested loops over `i < j < k` do one step per triple of different positions:

```formula
W_3(n) = n(n − 1) × (n − 2) / 6
W_3(n) ≈ n^3 / 6 = Θ(n^3)
where
W_3(n): the number of steps the three nested loops take
n: the input size
≈: approximately equal to, for large n
Θ(n^3): Big-Theta of n cubed: grows at exactly the rate of n × n × n, up to a constant factor
In words: there are about a sixth of n cubed ways to choose three positions in order, which is still cubic.
```

> [!tip] A quick sanity check
> For nested loops, ask "roughly how many times does the innermost line run, as a fraction of the full box?" If it's a constant fraction (a half, a sixth), the class is the same as the full product.

## Key takeaways
- Sequential blocks add; independent nested counts multiply.
- When the inner bound depends on the outer variable, sum the actual counts.
- A function call contributes the work of its body, rather than a single free step.

## Further reading
- [TimeComplexity — Python wiki](https://wiki.python.org/moin/TimeComplexity)
- [Algorithms by Jeff Erickson (free textbook)](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/)


lessons.title: Doubling and growing inner loops
lessons.summary: Recognise logarithmic loops and sum a geometric series of inner-loop lengths.
lessons.body:
Here n is the positive input size. Do not multiply the largest possible inner count by every outer pass without checking how the inner length changes.

## Logarithmic loops

A loop whose variable is **multiplied or divided** by a constant each step runs a logarithmic number of times.

```python
# For n = 17, i finishes at 32.
i = 1
while i < n:
    i *= 2
```

`i` takes the values 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., stopping once it reaches n. Count the steps:

```formula
i = 2^k
2^k ≥ n
k = ⌈log_2(n)⌉
k = ⌈log_2(16)⌉ = 4
k = ⌈log_2(17)⌉ = ⌈4.09⌉ = 5
where
i: the loop variable, which doubles every pass, so after k passes it equals 2^k
k: the number of loop iterations; the loop stops at the first k with 2^k ≥ n
n: the input size, the value the loop counts up to
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n, the power you raise 2 to in order to get n
⌈x⌉: ceiling: round x up to the next whole number
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: doubling from 1 reaches n after about log_2(n) steps, rounded up.
```

For a bound of 16, the loop has four passes through 1, 2, 4 and 8; a bound of 17 requires a fifth pass.

The same logarithmic growth holds for halving (`n //= 2`) or another fixed factor. Tripling uses a base-three logarithm, but fixed log bases differ only by a constant factor. Here n is the positive input bound. This is the shape behind binary search and balanced trees.

A loop that stops at a square root is different again:

```python
# For n = 9, i finishes at 4.
i = 1
while i * i <= n:
    i += 1
```

This loop stops when the square of its variable passes the bound, so its iteration count follows the square root. A bound of a million gives about a thousand iterations. Here is that count, followed by the independent-loop product:

## Mixed loops and two classic traps

```formula
K(n) = ⌊√(n)⌋
K(1000000) = 1000
W(n) = n⌈log_2(n)⌉
where
K(n): the square-root loop’s iteration count
W(n): the number of doublings in the nested example below
n: the positive whole-number loop bound
√: the nonnegative square root
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down
⌈ ⌉: ceiling: round up
log_2: the base-2 logarithm
In words: The first loop counts up to the square root; restarting a doubling loop on every outer pass multiplies its count by the input size.
```

A linear outer loop around an independently restarted logarithmic inner loop has Θ(n log n) work, where n is its bound:

```python
for i in range(n):        # n times
    # Restart the doubling for every i.
    j = 1
    while j < n:          # log n times
        j *= 2
```

Now the trap. What about an outer loop that **doubles** with an inner loop that runs `i` times?

```python
i = 1
while i < n:
    # Inner lengths are 1, 2, 4, 8, ...
    for j in range(i):
        work()
    i *= 2
```

Multiplying the logarithmic outer count by the maximum inner length would overestimate it. The actual inner lengths double from one through the last power of two below the bound. Adding them gives a **geometric series**, dominated by its last term:

```formula
W = 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2^k
W = 2^{k+1} − 1
2^k < n,  so  W < 2n
n = 100:  W = 1 + … + 64 = 127
where
W: the total number of work() calls
k: the number of the last outer pass; on that pass i = 2^k, the largest power of 2 below n
n: the input size
…: "and so on"
In words: each power of 2 is one more than the sum of all the smaller ones, so the whole sum is just under twice the last term, and the last term is less than n.
```

So the whole thing is **Θ(n)**. Always sum the actual counts.

## Key takeaways
- Multiplying a loop variable by a fixed factor gives logarithmic iteration counts.
- Resetting an inner loop makes each outer pass pay its cost again.
- Growing inner lengths can form a geometric series whose largest term dominates.

## Further reading
- [Algorithms by Jeff Erickson (free textbook)](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/)

Here n is the positive input size. This example varies the step of the inner range instead of varying its endpoint.

## A harmonic loop

The second trap is the **harmonic** loop:

```python
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    # i is the step; the stop n is excluded.
    for j in range(0, n, i):
        work()
```

The inner range starts at zero, stops before the bound and jumps by the outer variable’s value. Its count is the input bound divided by that step, rounded up. Sum those actual counts:

```formula
W(n) ≈ n/1 + n/2 + n/3 + … + n/n
W(n) ≈ n H(n)
H(n) = 1 + 1/2 + … + 1/n ≈ ln(n)
W(1000) ≈ 1000 × 7.5 = 7500
W(n) = Σ_{i=1}^{n} ⌈n/i⌉
W(1000) = 8053
where
W(n): the total number of work() calls
n: the input size
H(n): the n-th harmonic number, the sum of the fractions 1/1 to 1/n
ln(n): the natural logarithm of n (base e ≈ 2.718); about 0.69 × log_2(n)
…: "and so on"
≈: approximately equal to (each pass runs n / i times rounded up; H(1000) ≈ 7.49)
Σ_{i=1}^{n}: sum over all step sizes from one through the bound
i: the positive step size set by the outer loop
⌈ ⌉: ceiling: round up to a whole number of iterations
In words: the inner loop shrinks as 1/i, and those fractions add up to only about the logarithm of n, so the total is about n log n, not n squared.
```

So this is **Θ(n log n)**, where n is the input bound, rather than quadratic. Similar sums appear in sieves; the Sieve of Eratosthenes has the tighter Θ(n log log n) bound, where the second logarithm is applied to the first. They also occur in graph and number-theory problems.

| Pattern | Approximate count |
|---|---|
| Inner bound grows with outer | half the square |
| Doubling variable | logarithmic |
| Squared variable within bound | square root |
| Doubling outer, inner to outer | less than twice the bound |
| Inner step equals outer | bound times natural log |

## Key takeaways
- A range step can change the inner length even when the stop stays fixed.
- The harmonic loop adds many shrinking contributions rather than equally sized passes.
- Summing actual counts can reveal a tighter bound than multiplying maximum bounds.

## Further reading
- [Harmonic series — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_series_(mathematics))
- [Algorithms by Jeff Erickson (free textbook)](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/)

lessons.title: Recursive work and hidden costs
lessons.summary: Count recursive calls and uncover work hidden inside ordinary Python operations.
lessons.body:
Here n is the input size or recursive argument. A small amount of source code can describe a large amount of executed work.

## Recursion

For recursive code, count **how many calls** happen and **how much work each does** outside the recursive calls.

Linear recursion makes one call per level:

```python
def fact(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return 1
    # Multiply after the smaller call ends.
    return n * fact(n - 1)
```

Θ(n) calls and multiplications in the unit-cost model, where n is the recursive argument. Actual Python multiplication gets more expensive as the factorial grows; factorial means the product of all positive integers up to the argument.

Branching recursion is where things explode. Naive Fibonacci makes two calls per level:

```python
# fib(5) returns 5; it makes 15 calls.
def fib(n):
    if n < 2:
        return n
    # Both branches can repeat earlier work.
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
```

Draw the **recursion tree**:

```
                 f5
           /            \
         f4              f3
       /    \          /    \
     f3      f2      f2      f1
    /  \    /  \    /  \
   f2  f1  f1  f0  f1  f0
  /  \
 f1  f0
```

(Here `f5` means `fib(5)`.) `fib(5)` makes 15 calls. In general:

```formula
calls(n) = 2F(n + 1) − 1
calls(5) = 2F(6) − 1 = 2 × 8 − 1 = 15
calls(n) = Θ(φ^n)
φ = (1 + √5) / 2 ≈ 1.618
where
calls(n): the total number of calls made by fib(n), counting the first one
F(n): the n-th Fibonacci number: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, … (each is the sum of the two before; F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1, F(6) = 8)
n: the argument passed to fib
φ: phi, the golden ratio, about 1.618
φ^n: n copies of φ multiplied together
√5: the square root of 5, about 2.236
Θ: Big-Theta: grows at exactly this rate, up to a constant factor
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the number of calls is itself almost twice a Fibonacci number, and Fibonacci numbers grow by a factor of about 1.618 each step, so the call count grows exponentially.
```

`fib(30)` makes about 2.7 million calls; `fib(50)` would make about 4 × 10^10.

The waste is visible in the tree: `fib(3)` is computed twice, `fib(2)` three times. Caching results (**memoisation**, covered with dynamic programming later) reduces this to n distinct calls: Θ(n).

Divide-and-conquer recursion (halving the problem) needs the tools in the recurrence lessons, but a rough guide:

- One call on half the input, O(1) extra work: Θ(log n) (binary search).
- Two calls on halves, O(n) extra work: Θ(n log n) (merge sort).

## Hidden costs

Many "one-line" operations aren't O(1). In this CPython table, n is the list length:

| Operation | Cost |
|---|---|
| `x in some_list` | O(n) |
| `x in some_set` | O(1) average |
| `lst.append(x)` | O(1) amortised |
| `lst.insert(0, x)` | O(n) |
| `lst.pop(0)` | O(n) |
| `lst[a:b]` | O(b - a) copy |
| `sorted(lst)` | O(n log n) |
| `len(lst)` | O(1) |

This turns innocent-looking code quadratic:

```python
# unique([3, 1, 3]) returns [3, 1].
def unique(items):
    seen = []
    out = []
    for x in items:
        if x not in seen:   # O(n) scan
            seen.append(x)
            out.append(x)
    return out
```

The membership test scans `seen`, so the function is Θ(n^2) when most items are distinct. Changing `seen` to a `set` makes it Θ(n) on average. The algorithm didn't change; the data structure did.

> [!warning] Slicing in recursion
> `binary_search(arr[mid:], target)` looks logarithmic, but each slice copies the chosen half. The shrinking halves add to just under the original length, so a search on n items is O(n) rather than O(log n). Pass indices (`lo`, `hi`) instead.

```formula
C(n) ≈ n/2 + n/4 + n/8 + …
C(n) < n
where
C(n): the copied element slots over an absent-target search
n: the original list length
…: continue halving
≈: approximately, ignoring integer rounding
<: less than
In words: The series of copied halves is linear in the original length.
```

## Key takeaways
- Count all recursive calls and the work performed outside those calls.
- Naive Fibonacci repeats subproblems; memoisation stores their answers.
- Membership tests and slices can turn a short-looking Python function into expensive work.

## Further reading
- [TimeComplexity — Python wiki](https://wiki.python.org/moin/TimeComplexity)
- [Memoization — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memoization)
- [Algorithms by Jeff Erickson (free textbook)](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/)
